s: The people of Indus Valley believed in –

s: The beginning of idol worship is to be considered in –

s:
Which of the following characterizes/characterize the people of Indus Civilization?
1. They possessed great places and temples.
2. They worshipped, both male and female deities.
3. They employed horse-drawn chariots in warfare.
Select the correct answer using the code given below
x: Only 2 is correct: the Harappans worshipped both male (Pashupati) and female (Mother Goddess) deities. No palaces or temples have been found, and horse-drawn chariots are a Vedic, not Harappan, feature (UPSC 2013 key: b).

s: Worship of Devi Mata was related to
x: Devi Mata (Mother Goddess) worship is a Harappan (Indus Valley) cult, shown by terracotta female figurines; it later survives in Shakti cults.

s: The Indus valley people worshipped
x: The Indus people worshipped a proto-Shiva (Pashupati) figure; Indra and Varuna are Rig Vedic gods, and Brahma and Vishnu are later deities.

s: The shape of which tree is found in the seals from the Indus Civilization?
x: The pipal is the tree most often shown on Indus seals (e.g. a deity standing among pipal branches); the pipal motif goes back to the Early Harappan phase.

s: Which of the following birds was worshipped by the Harappa People?
x: NextGen lists the pigeon (dove) among the Harappans' sacred symbols, so pigeon is right; the peacock appears only as a pottery motif, and crow and eagle are not attested.

s: A horned deity engraved on a terracotta cake has been recovered from
x: A triangular terracotta cake from Kalibangan carries a horned deity on one side and a human dragging a goat (animal sacrifice) on the other; Kalibangan also has a row of seven fire altars.

s:
The worship of Fire in the Indus valley is proved by the discovery of the Fire altar at

a. Surkotada
b. Alamgirpur

c. Kalibangan
d. Chanhudaro
x: Fire altars were found at Kalibangan (seven in a row) and Lothal (also Banawali, Rakhigarhi), not at Surkotada or Chanhudaro – so 'c only'.

s: The late Harappan cultures are primarily Chalcolithic in which tools of stone and copper are used. 5. II. They do not show metal objects requiring complicated casting. III. The Chalcolithic people in the later Harappan phase lived in villages. IV. In the late Harappan phase at Bhagwanpura in Haryana, burnt bricks were not found.
x: I, II and III are correct: Late Harappan cultures were chalcolithic (stone and copper tools), lacked complex cast metal objects, and were village-based. IV is wrong: the Late Harappan people at Bhagwanpura lived in burnt-brick houses (some baked bricks occur there).

s:
Which of the following statements about Harappa Civilisation is/are correct?

I. There is the extraordinary uniformity in artefacts as evident in pottery seals, bricks and weights.

II. The late Harappa sites also maintained the same construction techniques as were used in mature Harappa sites.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
x: Only I: the extraordinary uniformity of pottery, seals, bricks and weights is a Mature Harappan trait. In the Late Harappan phase seals, script, weights and brick standards lost this uniformity, so II is wrong.

s:
With reference to the difference between the culture of Rigvedic Aryans and Indus valley people, which of the following statements is/are correct?

s: 'Sabha' of Vedic-era –
o: Was an institution of mercantile people of the villages
National Assembly of all the people of the state
x:
Most books and keys: council of ministers. Strictly: a select council of elders/nobles with judicial work, later close to a royal court (PMF A&M Part 1 p.128).
The Sabha was a small, select council of elders and nobles that advised the Rajan (and judged disputes), the closest option being a council of ministers. The 'assembly of all the people' was the Samiti; the Sabha was not a mercantile body.

s: In which Veda are Sabha and Samiti declared as separate institutions?
x: Sabha and Samiti appear in the Rig Veda, but the Atharvaveda explicitly treats them as two separate institutions, the 'two daughters of Prajapati'.

s: In which of the Vedas, Sabha and Samiti are called as two daughters of Prajapati ?
x: The Atharvaveda calls the Sabha and the Samiti the two daughters of Prajapati.

s: The Rigvedic tribal assembly associated with judicial function was
x: The Sabha, a select body of elders, also performed judicial functions; the Samiti was the general tribal assembly that chose the chief, and the Vidatha was mainly a religious-military gathering.

s: The administrative setup of early Aryans was in the nature of?
x: The early Aryans had a kinship-based tribal polity: the Rajan was a tribal chief, protector of the tribe and cattle, with no fixed territory or standing army.

s: The System of Governance prevalent in the Vedic era was

s: Who was the officer in-charge of Pastoral Lands in Rigvedic period?

s: The staple food of the Vedic Aryan was
x: Milk and its products (ghee, curd) were the staple food of the Vedic Aryans of a cattle-based economy; barley was the main grain, rice and pulses came later.

s: In the ancient period chief-livelihood of the Aryans was
x:

Of the options, agriculture: the Aryans combined cattle-rearing with farming, and in the Later Vedic age agriculture became the chief livelihood. Pastoralism (the early Rig Vedic mainstay) is not offered; hunting, craft and business were minor.

s: This was the status of an Indian woman in the Vedic period
x: Women in the (Rig) Vedic age enjoyed a relatively good status – education, choice of husband, attendance at assemblies, no child marriage – within a patriarchal society, so 'somewhat superior' (compared with later periods). 'Very low' fits later periods, and 'sororate' is a marriage custom, not a status.
